questions.prompt: The figure above shows the region $A$, which is bounded by the $x$- and $y$-axes, the graph of $f(x)=\frac{\sin x}{x}$ for $x>0$, and the vertical line $x=k$. If $k$ increases at a rate of $\frac{\pi}{4}$ units per second, how fast is the area of region $A$ increasing when $k=\frac{\pi}{6}$?

media.alt: A shaded region A bounded by the y-axis, x-axis, the curve y equals sine x divided by x, and the vertical line x equals k.
media.caption: Region A bounded by the coordinate axes, $y=\frac{\sin x}{x}$, and $x=k$.

questions.explanation: Let $A(k)=\int_0^k \frac{\sin x}{x}\,dx$. By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and the chain rule, $\frac{dA}{dt}=\frac{\sin k}{k}\frac{dk}{dt}$. At $k=\frac{\pi}{6}$ and $\frac{dk}{dt}=\frac{\pi}{4}$, this is $\frac{1/2}{\pi/6}\cdot\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{3}{4}$.
questions.workedSolution: Define the area by $A(k)=\int_0^k \frac{\sin x}{x}\,dx$. Differentiate with respect to time: $\frac{dA}{dt}=\frac{\sin k}{k}\frac{dk}{dt}$. Substituting $k=\frac{\pi}{6}$ gives $\frac{\sin(\pi/6)}{\pi/6}=\frac{1/2}{\pi/6}=\frac{3}{\pi}$. Therefore $\frac{dA}{dt}=\frac{3}{\pi}\cdot\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{3}{4}$ square units per second.
questions.alternativeSolution: At any instant, increasing the right boundary by $dk$ adds an approximate strip of area $f(k)dk$. Hence $\frac{dA}{dt}=f(k)\frac{dk}{dt}$, which gives the same result.
questions.noncalculatorSolution: Use the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and exact trigonometric values.
questions.studentExplanation: The instantaneous area growth equals the height of the region at $x=k$ times the speed of the moving boundary.
questions.teacherExplanation: This item assesses a geometric interpretation of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus combined with the chain rule.
commonMistakes: Stopping at $f(\pi/6)=\frac{3}{\pi}$ and forgetting to multiply by $\frac{dk}{dt}$.
Treating the area as a rectangle $kf(k)$.
